title: Who could be behind hoax bomb threats to European air travel?
description: The warnings came in thick and fast, targeting one airline or airport after another. In nearly all cases - London's Heathrow airport being a notable e
body: The warnings came in thick and fast, targeting one airline or airport after another. In nearly all cases - London's Heathrow airport being a notable exception - they were taken to be credible enough to divert the aircraft in question, or even in Italy's case, to scramble fighter jets to escort it. They all turned out to be false, which does not, of course, mean that the next ones will not  be real.It is hardly surprising that the simultaneous, co-ordinated nature of these airline hoaxes, coupled with other malicious actions across Europe, are causing some people to point the finger of suspicion at Russia. Following a series of cyber-attacks and mysterious drone sightings over sensitive sites earlier this year, in the past few days we have seen the remote hacking of supermarket freezers, as well as a blood bank, a suspicious incident on Poland's border with Russia, and in August a drone attack Germany's Leipzig Halle airport which its interior minister publicly blamed on Moscow.So is Russia behind this?There are many who argue, based purely on circumstantial evidence, that this must surely be yet another example of "hybrid", "grey zone" or "sub-threshold" warfare - actions that damage a nation's infrastructure or society but which tend to be anonymous, deniable and which fall short of triggering Nato's Article 5 and thereby mobilising a response by the West.Moscow is certainly furious with Nato for supporting Ukraine and, in doing so, frustrating the Kremlin's plans to swallow up that country and effectively terminate its independence. Russian bloggers have also suggested that, if Ukraine's drones are currently making Russia's airports unsafe, and Western sanctions are blocking Russian airlines from European airspace, then why shouldn't Western nations feel the same pain?But as of Thursday evening no hard evidence had emerged linking the airline hoaxes to Russia, Iran or any proxy groups controlled by them. There is the email threat sent on Thursday morning to airport authorities in Rome, purporting to be from "Fighters of the Male State". That name likely refers to the Russian group Muzhskoi Legion or "Male Legion", an ultra-right group with such extreme views it was banned by a Moscow court in 2021. Yet, it retained tens of thousands of online followers on Telegram as it cheered on the full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine in the following year.But the email sent to Rome, even if genuine - and who is to say it is not another group hiding behind that name? - is unlikely to provide the leads that police and airport authorities need to pin down who is generating these hoaxes and why.For national police forces, airport authorities and transport ministries trying to work out who is behind these hoaxes and how best to mitigate their effect when they happen again, the task is not to go with who they think might be the most likely culprits but instead to follow the cold, hard leads - if they can find them.

schema.headline: Who could be behind hoax bomb threats to European air travel?

title: British doctor infected with Ebola in DR Congo being treated at London hospital
description: Image caption, A large convey of emergency vehicles transported the man to the Royal Free Hospital in north LondonUpdated 21 minutes agoA British doct
body: Image caption, A large convey of emergency vehicles transported the man to the Royal Free Hospital in north LondonUpdated 21 minutes agoA British doctor who tested positive for Ebola in the Democratic Republic of Congo has been flown back to the UK.The man, who has not been identified, landed at RAF Northolt before being transported to a specialist infectious diseases unit at the Royal Free Hospital in north London.It is the first confirmed case of a UK national contracting Ebola during the most recent outbreak of the rare but deadly virus in DR Congo, which has so far led to more than 5,000 deaths.Dr Renu Bindra, deputy director of the All Hazards Public Health Response team at the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA), said there are "well-established procedures for dealing with cases like this" and the risk to the public remains low.The infected doctor was brought to the UK on a medical evacuation flight as part of a joint effort by the UK and DR Congo governments and their international health partners, the Department of Health (DoH) said. A convoy of emergency vehicles were on hand to complete the transfer following the man's arrival at the RAF base. Three large police vans travelled at either end of the convey, while two ambulances and another support car were involved.Traffic was stopped and police exited the vans to keep the public away as the convey arrived at the Royal Free Hospital. The man is now being treated in a "highly specialised"  isolation unit at the hospital, the DoH said. Image source, ReutersThe Royal Free Hospital successfully treated three health workers who had been evacuated after the Ebola outbreak in West Africa in 2014 and 2015.There have only been four confirmed cases of the virus in the UK - one, in 1976, resulting from a laboratory incident, and three involving health workers who were responding to an outbreak in West Africa between 2014 and 2015.None of these cases have resulted in a death. Image caption, The plane carrying the infected man arrived at RAF Northolt on ThursdayThere have been more than 10,000 confirmed cases since the recent outbreak in DR Congo started in May, which has grown to become the second most deadly recorded spate of infections, behind the outbreak in West Africa in the 2010s.The current outbreak in DR Congo has a fatality rate of 48.6% reported at the end of last month.Ebola can result in serious illness and death. Early symptoms include vomiting and diarrhoea but it can progress to organ failure and internal bleeding.The virus spreads from one person to another by contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit.The ongoing outbreak centred on DR Congo is fuelled by the Bundibugyo variant of the virus.There is no approved vaccine but the World Health Organization said experts have recommended adding two new candidate drugs to an ongoing clinical trial.The vaccines, one developed by the University of Oxford and the Serum Institute of India, and another by the firm Moderna, will join the trial once they are approved by Congolese health authorities.It will be the first time jabs specifically designed to protect against the Bundibugyo virus are tested during an outbreak.Since the outbreak, Ebola cases have also been confirmed in Kenya, Nigeria and Uganda.

schema.headline: British doctor infected with Ebola in DR Congo being treated at London hospital

title: Russell Brand is being investigated over two new rape complaints, police say
description: Image source, Zeynep Demir/Anadolu via Getty ImagesImage caption, Brand has been found guilty of rape and sexual assault, following a three-week trial
body: Image source, Zeynep Demir/Anadolu via Getty ImagesImage caption, Brand has been found guilty of rape and sexual assault, following a three-week trial at Southwark Crown Court ByHelena WilkinsonNews correspondentUpdated 5 hours agoWarning: Details of rape and sexual assaultRussell Brand is being investigated over rape allegations made by two more women, it can now be reported.The disgraced comedian has been found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault by a jury of eight men and four women at Southwark Crown Court, following a three-week trial.More victims are likely to come forward following his conviction, the detective who led the police investigation has said.Det Supt Andy Furphy, from the Metropolitan Police, said he hoped other women would gain "courage" and "confidence" from the guilty verdicts.Brand was found not guilty of two counts of rape and one count of attempted indecent assault.'Ruthless'Brand had initially been coy and quiet in police interviews, said Furphy, but became bolder as officers continued to question him."As he gets used to something, he becomes more emboldened by it," Furphy said. "You can certainly see that in his offending."Hundreds of people were interviewed as part of the investigation and officers said several witnesses came forward, some of whom had previously had a sexual relationship with Brand. Katy Perry, the US singer who was married to Brand from 2010 to 2012, was not interviewed.Brand, 51, who was described in court as "ruthless" and a "sexual predator", was once one of the UK's most high-profile and in-demand entertainers.Some of the women said they had been left "haunted for years" by what he did to them.Speaking to the BBC, officers working on the three-year Metropolitan Police investigation described how bringing Brand to justice was not without its challenges.Image source, Chris Jackson/Getty ImagesImage caption, Katy Perry, the US singer who was married to Brand from 2010 to 2012, was not interviewed by police as part of the investigation Allegations about Brand's behaviour first emerged in the media in September 2023.The Times, Sunday Times and Channel 4's Dispatches programme jointly reported that four women had accused him of rape, sexual assault and emotional abuse - claims he strongly denied.The investigation into other reports against Brand began soon after the story broke."We kind of assumed that people might want to come forward," Furphy said, "and people came forward."Victim reports were made to forces across the country and the Met set up a dedicated team of officers to lead the investigation, which it called Operation Actinolite. Officers said they have since taken more than 340 witness statements - including from Brand's former employers, his ex-colleagues and associates.One officer was assigned to read Brand's books, watch his stand-up routines and DVDs and listen to his podcasts to help build the case.Brand's high profile and the intense media scrutiny around him proved a challenge to officers, said Furphy.Another complexity for the team was the allegations were all "non-recent". The earliest dated back 27 years. It meant there was no CCTV and no forensic evidence to work with.  Furphy said police had to look for other ways to build their case."Can we look at where the victims were at the time? Who did they speak to in the aftermath of it? Did they tell anybody else? What other available material is there for us to review that might lend some weight to it? Just because it's non-recent doesn't mean that we can't solve it at all."A former friend of Brand's was called to court to give evidence for the prosecution, while a statement from the parents of one of the women was heard.The entertainer's former personal assistant, who worked closely with Brand, told the jury about his "insane sexual appetite".'Deeply uncomfortable' processTwo months after the police investigation began, Brand was interviewed under caution for the first time. He was interviewed on two further occasions in the following months.In each interview he provided officers with a prepared statement, which said he did not recognise the complainants or recall the alleged incidents and that if any sexual activity had taken place, it would have been consensual. He then answered "no comment" to the officers' questions.Charges were brought against Brand in early April 2025: one count of rape, one count of oral rape, two charges of sexual assault and one allegation of indecent assault. The final charge would later be changed to attempted indecent assault at his trial.The charges all related to women who had come forward since the initial Channel 4 documentary.The following month he appeared at Westminster Magistrates' Court, in London. He was swarmed by camera crews, so much so that it took him more than two minutes to walk the short distance to the court door. At a later court hearing he pleaded not guilty to the charges.Meanwhile, women continued to come forward with more allegations.In July 2025, Brand was interviewed for a fourth time before being charged with further offences: one count of rape and one count of sexual assault. He also denied those allegations.And then on 14 October 2026, accompanied by his wife Laura, the actor and comedian entered the glass dock at London's Southwark Crown Court for the start of his trial.Image source, Leon Neal/Getty ImagesImage caption,  Brand arrives at court ahead of his trial, accompanied by his wife Laura  The women each came to court and gave evidence to the jury from behind a screen, with Brand listening from the dock. At times they cried as they gave their evidence.Furphy believes there may be more women who will now come forward."I think it's likely - potentially - that other women will come forward," he said. "They'll probably gain some courage and some confidence from what's happened in the courtroom over the last few weeks."He credits the women for their bravery during what has been at times a "deeply uncomfortable" process. "They are courageous, determined women and our focus has always been on them, not Russell Brand."Russell Brand on TrialYou can follow analysis and further insights on the BBC podcast Russell Brand on Trial - available on BBC Sounds, YouTube, iPlayer, or wherever you get your BBC podcasts

schema.headline: Russell Brand is being investigated over two new rape complaints, police say

title: Farage says he is worried Trump will step up Iran war after midterm 'disaster'
description: Nigel Farage has said he fears Donald Trump will "aggressively" continue his war with Iran after his "disaster" in the US midterm elections.The Reform
body: Nigel Farage has said he fears Donald Trump will "aggressively" continue his war with Iran after his "disaster" in the US midterm elections.The Reform UK leader said the US president was still a friend, but accused him of having "broke a promise" to the American electorate by launching the war.The war in Iran, which the US began in February 2026, weighed heavily in the midterm election results earlier this week in which the Democrats swept Trump's Republicans out of power in Congress.Farage, who had initially urged people to support the war, said that following the election results he worried Trump would respond with more strikes on Iran.Asked how he thinks President Trump will respond, Farage told broadcasters on Thursday: "I suppose I worry that the president will continue aggressively attacking Iran."That worries me because that would have even more serious implications for the price of oil, for inflation, for the whole western world".He acknowledged he had initially supported the war but stressed he "never supported endless war".Asked if the war was a mistake, he said: "There's no question about it."The US president had "always kept his promises," added Farage, but "in this case, he said no more foreign wars and here we are in month eight of a war with no sign of ending.""That and the resulting fuel prices are what in the end has done the damage."Trump said on Tuesday that the poor results for Republican congressional candidates were partly due to the war and the related surge in oil prices.But he insisted he did not regret launching a joint attack with Israel on Iran."Trump has had an amazing career - he has beaten the pollsters, he has gone way beyond expectations," he added."This was his last big election and they all say, that all political careers end in failure."His comments came at an event to announce Reform's first defence spokesperson, after the party was criticised for not having one.Angus MacIntyre said he had stood down from a 40-year military career, including as a Wing Commander in the Royal Air Force (RAF), to take on the role.MacIntyre pledged in a speech to end prosecutions of serving military personnel and veterans within the first 100 days of a Reform government.Defence Secretary Wes Streeting and Tory leader Kemi Badenoch had criticised Reform for lacking a defence spokesperson despite having dedicated posts for immigration, the economy and education.Farage said MacIntyre would form part of "a team we will build to represent us" on the issues of defence, security and cybersecurity.

schema.headline: Farage says he is worried Trump will step up Iran war after midterm 'disaster'

title: The Pitt and ER are similar enough for lawsuit to proceed, judge rules
description: US drama The Pitt is similar enough to medical series ER for a lawsuit against its producers to progress, a court in the US has ruled. The widow of Mi
body: US drama The Pitt is similar enough to medical series ER for a lawsuit against its producers to progress, a court in the US has ruled. The widow of Michael Crichton, who created ER, argues The Pitt is effectively a reboot of the series, which has been made without proper permission or credit. Sherri Crichton says her husband's contract included a "frozen rights" provision that prohibited any spin-offs, sequels or reboots of ER being made without his express consent.A three-judge panel said there are "clear and numerous similarities between The Pitt and ER," which means the case can go ahead. Warner Bros previously described the lawsuit as "baseless" and sought to have it dismissed.Listing the similarities between the two shows, the court cited the emergency room setting, the fast pace, use of medical jargon, graphic depictions of injuries, and younger doctors fresh from medical school being trained. "We find the details here suffice for a prima facie case," the judges said.It means the case will now go to a jury trial in Los Angeles Superior Court.But the judges dismissed separate claims against actor-producer Noah Wyle, executive producer John Wells and showrunner R Scott Gemmill.The justices said there was insufficient evidence to show the three producers were aware they could be violating Crichton's contractual rights.ER launched in 1994, based on original screenplay written by Crichton. It starred George Clooney, Anthony Edwards, Eriq La Salle and Maria Bello, and aired 331 episodes over the next 15 years.The show, which followed a group of doctors working in an emergency room in Chicago, was a hit with viewers and critics, and won 23 Emmy Awards during its run including outstanding drama series.Discussions about a possible reboot of the show began in 2020, and studio Warner Bros spent months negotiating with Crichton's estate.Those talks were reported to have collapsed over credit and financial guarantees, and producers began developing The Pitt in its place.But Sherri Crichton and the John Michael Crichton Trust argue the show is a rebranded but uncredited reboot of ER, using the same formula, pacing, style and setting, rather than an entirely original series. They said producers "simply moved the show from Chicago to Pittsburgh, rebranded it The Pitt, and ploughed ahead without any attribution or compensation for Crichton and his heirs". Many actors and creatives from ER also work on The Pitt, including Wyle, Gemmill and Wells.After legal action began in 2024, Warner Bros Television said in a statement that the lawsuit was "baseless", arguing that The Pitt was a "new and original show", adding that the studio would "vigorously defend against these meritless claims".But in a 33-page opinion published on Wednesday, a three-judge panel unanimously upheld an earlier ruling that Crichton's estate had presented enough evidence to pursue its claim. Warner Bros had sought to have the lawsuit dismissed on appeal, arguing the shows shared only "generic similarities" common to "any dramatic story involving emergency room doctors".The judges said they had compared the opening episode scripts for the two shows and found sufficient similarities in plot, themes, dialogue, mood, setting, pace, characters, graphic injury detail and sequence of events. Sherri Crichton said: "I am deeply gratified by the Court of Appeal decision and look forward to discovery and to our case, which affects writers, creators, and their families and estates, being presented to a jury."Warner Bros has not yet commented on the latest ruling.

schema.headline: The Pitt and ER are similar enough for lawsuit to proceed, judge rules

title: Vance walks Trump tightrope with scathing election critique blaming Iran war
description: Figure caption, With Congress flipped, what does Donald Trump do next?ByWashington correspondentUpdated 03:47 GMTVice-President JD Vance sent shockwav
body: Figure caption, With Congress flipped, what does Donald Trump do next?ByWashington correspondentUpdated 03:47 GMTVice-President JD Vance sent shockwaves through Washington on Wednesday by blaming his party's midterm defeat squarely on the Iran war, in what was widely interpreted as an effort to distance himself from President Donald Trump ahead of a potential 2028 White House run.In a carefully calibrated, 600-word statement on X, the vice-president acknowledged that Trump's 2024 voters had deserted Republicans in the midterm election."The reason we lost is the war," he wrote. "The president himself said so last night."In interviews late Tuesday night and Wednesday, Trump had defended the war but acknowledged that it played a factor in Democrats flipping control of the US House of Representatives and the Senate.Vance's view on the war in Iran is an open secret in Washington.  While he has repeatedly backed the conflict since the US and Israel attacked Tehran in February, he has reportedly expressed opposition in private meetings with administration officials.But those disagreements had been kept out of the public eye - until now.Figure caption, Could Democrats in Congress end the war in Iran?Hours after Trump and the party were handed a bruising election defeat, Vance made clear that he felt the decision to go to war was a clear political mistake."If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest," Vance said.It was a striking statement, and one with no recent precedent: it's hard to recall a similar moment in recent US political history when a sitting vice-president has so sharply broken with the president on a signature foreign policy issue.Then came an arguably even greater surprise: Trump - who typically demands steadfast loyalty from his senior advisers - agreed with Vance that the midterms were "largely" decided by the war. He added that he would "do it again" if given the same choices.Image source, ReutersDrawing contrasts with Trump will be a delicate balancing act if Vance seeks the presidency, Byman added.That balance was on display in Vance's post. The vice president didn't mention Trump by name and attributed much of his election results analysis to unnamed pollsters.Vance "put his toe in the water to see what he's going to do," Ashley Davis, a Republican strategist, told the BBC.Beyond the Iran war criticism, Vance also offered a political roadmap that could preview a possible presidential campaign. He distilled the party's strategy to win back voters into a neat four-point gameplan:  "1) End the war 2) Focus on cost of living/inflation 3) Put America First 4) Change our relationship to Israel."The list encapsulated much of Vance's worldview since bursting onto the national political scene, and read like the core argument in a future stump speech.The BBC has contacted Vance's office for comment.Of course, the next presidential election is still two years away. Vance is expected to run but hasn't made an official decision, and aides insist that he's still mulling it over.It's also up for debate exactly how much Vance broke from Trump. Vance showed the message to Trump before posting it online, according to The New York Times.Trump, for his part, could change his mind and make clear he'll brook no dissent from Vance or anyone else.The president has been circumspect about who he'd support to succeed him as the 2028 Republican presidential nominee. Trump has praised Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio on several occasions, but hasn't said when - or if – he'd make an endorsement.The president appears to relish the guessing game of who he'd back to carry on his political movement, even in the past floating the idea that he'd continue to a third term (which is barred by the US Constitution).Vance's midterms missive might not be that significant in the end. Or it could have been the starting gun for the 2028 race and the battle for the post-Trump Republican Party.Nardine Saad contributed reporting.

schema.headline: Vance walks Trump tightrope with scathing election critique blaming Iran war

title: Cristiano Ronaldo retirement: Why has Portugal legend retired from international game?
description: Cristiano Ronaldo's old rival Leo Messi left Argentina less than a month ago with a nation applauding him.The Portugal legend has gone another way, an
body: Cristiano Ronaldo's old rival Leo Messi left Argentina less than a month ago with a nation applauding him.The Portugal legend has gone another way, and it was always going to be the case.The 41-year-old announced his international retirement after 23 years but also after a fallout with coach Jorge Jesus which was resolved with a sanction of 30 days, that had already been served, and a fine of 255 euros.It was the punishment imposed on the Portuguese striker for leaving the team's training camp without permission. Jesus kept him on the bench for one match and said he did not plan to start him in the next, so Ronaldo went home.His last appearance came on 24 September against Wales. He ends his international career with 146 goals in 234 games.A message went around Portugal with a big thank you for everything, calling Ronaldo a global ambassador and an inspiration to millions. Even so, the way it ended leaves a bit of a bitter taste.Was he going to be named in the next squad? Possibly, as Jesus said the door was open and the decision was Ronaldo's. What is clear is that he was no longer an automatic starter, and Cristiano has never handled that well.So is this another hissy fit? Partly, yes. He reacted the way he always has when a coach questions his place. But the label hides how much he adapted over the years.Such a pattern appears with almost every man who sat on the Portuguese bench - there were clashes, but also communion with managers and team-mates that help explain this ending.When a young Ronaldo first joined the squad, he arrived at camp with his baseball cap on backwards, enormous sunglasses and headphones turned up so loud they could be heard from a distance.He would not take the cap off to eat among veterans like Luis Figo and Rui Costa. Luiz Felipe Scolari saw an extraordinary player who was immature and obsessed with showing off. He reprimanded him in public, then told him privately that if he changed his attitude, he would one day captain Portugal.The first great disappointment came early, and it came at home. At 19, Ronaldo played in the final of Euro 2004 at the Estadio da Luz in Lisbon, in front of a country that had convinced itself the trophy was already on its way.A single headed goal by Angelos Charisteas was enough for unfancied Greece to win it by surprise. When the final whistle went, Ronaldo could not hold back the tears, and the image of the teenager crying on his own pitch travelled everywhere.It was a painful way to learn what a final costs, and it left him with a hunger that never really went away.Figo owned the number 7 at the time, so Ronaldo had to have 17. Figo helped him settle but had no intention of making it easy. When he left the national team in 2006, the shirt and the team became Ronaldo's.In September 2005, before a qualifier in Russia, Scolari and Figo went to his room to tell him his father had died. Scolari offered to send him home. Ronaldo chose to play, asked his team-mates to behave as normal, and spent time in the dressing room doing ball tricks.That was his way to cope with the expected but still hugely hurtful passing of his alcoholic dad.  He later called Scolari "father". That way the national team had become the place that held him together.Things went sour with Carlos Queiroz. After the 2010 World Cup exit against Spain, asked to explain a poor performance, Ronaldo told journalists to ask the coach. His influence in the camp had grown so large it changed routines and habits, which explains why the coach felt undermined.The sociologist Joao Nuno Coelho offers the best lens on how Portugal sees him. In his analysis, the national team became a representation of Portuguese identity and of the country's need to be seen internationally.In years of economic hardship and a crisis of confidence, a team that won admiration abroad was important beyond football.Ronaldo stood at the centre of that need and created contradictory feelings. Some Portuguese questioned his individualism and his ego, and not everyone saw themselves in his personality.Coelho explains criticising him became more difficult as time went by. The country wanted to be proud of him and sometimes felt uneasy at the same time.The former international Jorge Andrade told me some supporters preferred figures like Figo, Eusebio, Paulo Futre or Rui Costa. Even so, Portugal was proud to have him. And with the titles, the doubts eased.Under Fernando Santos in 2016, he changed. He accepted playing as a centre forward next to Nani - he had never taken a coach's instructions so naturally.After the opening draw with Iceland, he told Nani in private that he trusted Santos, and the dressing room began to see a real captain. After missing a penalty against Austria, he barely slept. Santos woke up and found him already awake.At the training camp in Marcoussis, he took a fan's megaphone and told supporters Portugal had won nothing yet. He was enjoying the leadership role.In the final in Paris, he left the pitch in tears, injured. He had not had the best tournament, with a muscle complaint that did not let him perform at his best.Nani took the armband. At half-time Ronaldo pulled himself together to encourage his team-mates, and before extra time, still limping, he told Eder he would score.And Eder did.But the old instinct never fully disappeared. During extra-time, Ronaldo stood in the technical area giving orders until the fourth official sent him back. Other coaches I consulted found it excessive.His greatest strength, the need to influence every result, also made limits hard to accept.When he debuted in 2003, Portugal was still searching for its first major title. Some players mark an era, and others change a national team for good. He belongs to the second group.That night in July 2016 gave Portugal its first European Championship.Three years later he scored a hat-trick against Switzerland to put them into the first Nations League final, which Portugal won. In 2025 he lifted a second Nations League at an age when most players have retired.No one has scored more goals for a national side, and no one has pulled on the Portugal shirt more times.Under his influence, Portugal stopped being a gifted team and became one that arrives at every tournament expecting to contend, while a whole generation of players came through a dressing room where he decided what the standard was.Coelho's point holds here as well: a small country found a way to be noticed, and for two decades he was its face.After 2016 the question around him changed. Fewer asked whether he was selfish, and more asked whether Portugal depended on him too much.In the World Cup in 2018, he scored three against Spain, including a free-kick after 45 attempts in major tournaments, and the team still went out to Uruguay.After a difficult 2026 World Cup, much was made of him still starting up front when in fact statistically that was his best period.Under Roberto Martinez, with 28 goals in 37 games, 0.756 per match, improves the 0.624 with Santos.The federation has announced a special tribute to honour his contribution, and that is necessary as the exit has not left fans room for a celebration they want to be part of.Not only they grew up with him, he took them to places they had not yet been.

schema.headline: Cristiano Ronaldo retirement: Why has Portugal legend retired from international game?

title: Jodie Burrage 'doesn't fear for safety' over online abuse 'because I get so much'
description: After struggling with her blood pressure as she lost her first WTA Tour singles match for 16 months, Jodie Burrage checked in with three things: a doc
body: After struggling with her blood pressure as she lost her first WTA Tour singles match for 16 months, Jodie Burrage checked in with three things: a doctor, a physiotherapist, and her phone.On her social media feed there were already messages promising punishment - and others making threats on her life - for losing 3-6 6-3 7-5 to Indian wildcard Vaishnavi Adkar."I try not to actually read what they say," Burrage told BBC Sport from Chennai, where she is still competing in the doubles."Because we are so used to it - which is really quite sad - I don't fear for my safety."You've got to have thick skin. There was some brutal stuff that was said, but I don't take it to heart."Sometimes it hurts more than others. If you've already got other stuff going on, or you're not in a great place, and that is put on top of everything else - this tour is tricky enough as it is."Burrage, who says her blood pressure "tanked" towards the end of the match, decided to share screenshots of the abuse on Instagram to raise awareness of an everyday problem for professional players."It happens every match - whether it's win or lose," the 27-year-old Briton said."Playing in Wrexham [on the World Tennis Tour last month], I won three matches [and] lost one. But after every single match there was some sort of abuse."I think that's where tennis players get it pretty hard - because in tennis you can bet on so many things."Abuse of players, particularly by angry gamblers, is not a new problem.Burrage's compatriot Katie Boulter shared with the BBC last year the abuse and death threats she received on a near-daily basis.This year's WTA and World Tennis report into online abuse, which was based on data from the Signify Group's Threat Matrix service, said "angry gamblers" were responsible for 42% of all verified abuse detected during the 2025 season.It is why there is so much disquiet about the sponsorship deals some tournaments have struck with gambling firms.The Davis Cup, for example, has an official sports betting partner, while in August self-described "prediction-market platform" Kalshi signed a multi-year deal with the US Open.Burrage believes social media platforms "should do more to help"."I think an ID should be put on every Instagram account, and then that way it makes more people more accountable for their actions on that platform," she said."I think it would limit what people would say. People should be accountable for what they say and that's where I think there could be more of a push to change. "It's only getting worse."All WTA and World Tennis players have access to Threat Matrix's services, which monitor all social media posts directed at players. The first aim is to provide a rapid assessment of whether an individual's safety is under threat. They can then alert the platforms, and potentially law enforcement agencies, to the offending content.Names can also be shared with gaming companies, so they have the option of banning offenders from their platforms.The service can extend to direct messages and even the moderation of accounts, so players never see the message in the first place. But this is not foolproof - and players may feel they would rather know about any threats made against them.Burrage has recently been able to improve her singles ranking to 474, from a low of 888 in July. Injury prevented her playing singles for nine months and when she returned for the grass court season, sickness held her back.But she will not allow the abuse to throw her off course."I'm at a place where it's all bigger picture for me and everything I'm doing now is to have a good season in 2027," she added."I'm building a team that is really good around me. They know where I've been, what I've gone through."It's not what you want, but if I have to go through it, then I will."

schema.headline: Jodie Burrage 'doesn't fear for safety' over online abuse 'because I get so much'

title: Jesus de Miguel: Funeral of Tenerife forward takes place as family thankful for support
description: Jesus de Miguel's family said "the mark he has left on so many people" was something they would always remember as the footballer's funeral took place
body: Jesus de Miguel's family said "the mark he has left on so many people" was something they would always remember as the footballer's funeral took place on Thursday.The Tenerife forward, who was 30, died after suffering a serious injury during a Spanish second division match on Monday.After colliding with FC Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono, De Miguel lay motionless on the pitch while being treated by medical staff and was taken to hospital, where he died at 07:00 GMT on Tuesday.Owono was sent off for the challenge and the game was abandoned.De Miguel's funeral was held in his parents' hometown of Navahermosa, Toledo, about 125km from the Spanish capital Madrid.His Tenerife team-mates carried his coffin before the service at San Miguel Arcangel.Current Spain coach Luis de la Fuente was among the mourners, along with Real Madrid president Florentino Perez, Atletico Madrid chief executive Miguel Angel Gil Marin and former Real and Spain coach Jose Antonio Camacho.De Miguel's agent, Manuel Hernandez, issued a statement on behalf of the family, which read: "Thank you for loving him, for remembering him and for being with us."We cannot find enough words to thank you for every message, every phone call and every gesture of affection we are receiving."Feeling such affection for Jesus and seeing the mark he has left on so many people is something we will always carry with us."Jesus leaves a void that is impossible to fill, but also cherished memories for all of us who were fortunate enough to share our lives with him."Tributes have been paid to De Miguel, who joined Tenerife in the summer of 2025, with a minute's silence being held at all games in European competitions this week.In a statement issued by his club Andorra on Wednesday, goalkeeper Owono said he was experiencing "the most difficult days of my life"."I feel enormous pain over the loss of Jesus," he added. "I think of him, his family, and everyone who loved him."The family also asked "with the utmost respect, that our privacy - and that of everyone who is supporting us at this time - be respected".In the hours after the death was announced, mourners laid flowers and lit candles beneath a black and white image of De Miguel at the Estadio Heliodoro Rodriguez Lopez - the stadium on the island of Tenerife, where Monday's game took place."We need to grieve in the peace and quiet that this situation demands," the statement added."We appreciate the affection, concern and expressions of support that his loss is inspiring, and we are deeply grateful to you all."

title: Henry Nowak's killer has sentence increased to 25 years
description: Image source, Police handoutImage caption, Vickrum Digwa must serve at least 24 years and 190 days before he can be considered for paroleByStuart Rust
body: Image source, Police handoutImage caption, Vickrum Digwa must serve at least 24 years and 190 days before he can be considered for paroleByStuart RustSouth of EnglandUpdated 2 hours agoA man jailed for life for murdering Henry Nowak has had his minimum prison term increased to 25 years by the Court of Appeal.Vickrum Digwa was serving a minimum of 21 years for stabbing 18-year-old student Nowak with a large dagger in Belmont Road, Southampton, on 3 December 2025.The Attorney General referred the case to the Court of Appeal on the grounds it was "unduly lenient", while Digwa also challenged his jail term as "manifestly excessive".The Lady Chief Justice quashed the sentence, ruling the original term "did not adequately reflect the overall seriousness of the murder".Digwa, who was also refused permission to appeal, told police Henry had attacked and racially abused him, which led to Henry, from Chafford Hundred in Essex, being handcuffed as he lay dying. The trial judge later found Digwa's accusations of racism to be a lie. Then 22, he was jailed for life at Southampton Crown Court in June.Image source, Family photoImage caption, Henry Nowak, 18, was fatally stabbed in Southampton in December 2025Both appeals were heard on Thursday by Lady Chief Justice Baroness Carr, Mr Justice Nicklin and Mr Justice Wall, with Digwa appearing via video link from HMP Frankland.The Lady Chief Justice said the trial judge had been entitled to start at 15 years, as he found Digwa had not taken the knife to the scene intending to commit a crime.But she said a "very significant uplift" was needed because of the use of the large kirpan.Figure caption, Henry Nowak’s killer has minimum term increased to 25 yearsA kirpan is a religious knife which baptised Sikhs are expected to carry at all times, and the law allows it to be carried in public for religious reasons.Digwa wore a small kirpan around his neck, but was also carrying a larger one on a belt, in keeping with an order of Sikhs known as the Nihang.The fact that initially carrying the knife may have been lawful "does not reduce the seriousness of its subsequent lethal use", she said.She said the original sentence had understated the repeated use of a large dagger with intent to kill, and the "deliberate cruelty, additional suffering and obstruction" that followed."It was not only lenient, but unduly so," she said.With time spent on remand deducted, Digwa must serve at least 24 years and 190 days before he can be considered for parole.Image source, ITV NewsImage caption, Henry's father, Mark Nowak and the rest of his family said they had been given "a life sentence of grief"In a statement, Henry's family called the decision "an important step towards justice" but said "no sentence, however long, can ever give Henry his life back".They continued: "We have been given a life sentence of grief. There is no appeal for us, no reduction in our suffering and no prospect of ever getting our son back."They said their "fight for justice is far from over" and that they would support an independent rapid review being carried out by Alex Chalk.Attorney General Ellie Reeves said: "The brutality and cruelty of this case horrified me, and I know that feeling is shared by the British public."My thoughts remain with Henry's family and loved ones at this incredibly difficult time. "No sentence can ever fill the void left by his loss, and I hope this outcome goes some way towards bringing them the justice they deserve."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Attorney General Ellie Reeves referred the sentence to the Court of Appeal under the Unduly Lenient Sentence schemeDuring the hearing, Jonathan Polnay KC, for the Attorney General, argued the 21-year term did not sufficiently reflect "the very high degree of seriousness of the offending".He said Digwa had abused the legal exemption allowing Sikhs to carry religious blades, which permitted him to have the dagger, and that this was "on at least one level analogous to an abuse of trust".Imran Khan KC, defending, argued the trial judge had counted overlapping aggravating factors more than once."To put it pithily, the Attorney General says 21 years was too little. We say it was too much," he said.The judges agreed some factors should not have counted against Digwa, including the community impact of the case, which he had not anticipated or intended.Digwa's mother, Kiran Kaur, was jailed for three years in July for assisting an offender by removing the knife from the scene. She abandoned an appeal against her sentence shortly before Thursday's hearing.Digwa has also applied to appeal against his murder conviction, which will be decided separately.Get in touchYour Voice

schema.headline: Henry Nowak's killer has sentence increased to 25 years

title: Could this be the last Bonfire Night for noisy fireworks?
description: Bangers, rockets and screamers have long been part of Bonfire Night - but the traditional celebrations might sound a little different next year.The go
body: Bangers, rockets and screamers have long been part of Bonfire Night - but the traditional celebrations might sound a little different next year.The government is currently considering reducing the noise limit for fireworks by 50% for those bought in shops for private use, after pressure from campaigners concerned about the impact on nervous animals and people with Post Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD).Professionally organised displays would continue to have no maximum limit provided the noise level is not harmful to human health.About 20 million people enjoy fireworks at home every year, according to industry figures.Andy Hubble, of the British Fireworks Association (BFA), said displays had already been getting quieter and a balance must be struck to prevent a black market in noisy fireworks springing up.The end of October sees the start of several celebrations traditionally marked by fireworks and bonfires, including Halloween on 31 October, Guy Fawkes Night on 5 November, and Diwali, which is on 8 November this year.The government has said an outright ban on the public buying fireworks would not be proportionate.But Business Minister Kate Dearden said her department was considering "reforms to fireworks legislation, focused on their key harms associated with their misuse - their noise, and contribution to antisocial behaviour – whilst still allowing individuals to enjoy fireworks safely and responsibly for the important community and cultural celebrations they play a part of."It is already illegal to sell fireworks to under 18s, or to set fireworks off after 23:00, with exemptions for special occasions including Bonfire Night, Diwali, New Year's Eve and Chinese New Year.But campaigners have raised concerns about the impact of loud bangs on nervous pets.Dog owner Katherine Alderson, from Clacton-on-Sea, told BBC Breakfast: "It's a nightmare every single year."This year I've actually barricaded my bedroom window with numerous layers of insulation to try and keep out the noise of fireworks."Asked whether reducing the bangs would take the fun out of fireworks, she said she believed displays "should be about the lights and colours" and suggested "a complete ban" on the sale of fireworks to the general public could be the solution.But other campaigners say a ban is not needed, including Alan Friggieri, from the charity Combat Stress, which supports veterans with PTSD.Giving evidence to MPs on the Commons' Business Committee, Friggieri said calls to their helpline jump at this time of year because loud bangs can trigger PTSD symptoms."Nothing quite sounds like an AK47 other than fireworks going off - it's that crackle," one veteran who had been shot multiple times had told him.Friggieri said veterans need to be able to plan around key dates, but he said he was not calling for a ban, because his organisation understands the cultural importance of firework displays.Calling for better enforcement of existing rules by police to stop antisocial behaviour, BFA vice chairman Hubble warned a ban in Ireland had seen a flourishing black market in firework sales. "There is a real risk here that if we make fireworks quieter that there is still a demand then we could create an illegal market where fireworks are coming in through internet sales and white van sales," he told BBC Breakfast."At the moment we have a really well-regulated market where we have enforcers that know the products and can test them but as soon as these products go undercover then we lose that."We could actually create a louder and noisier environment because those are the sorts of fireworks that we're seeing coming in through illegal sales on the internet."Asked whether it was true that displays were getting noisier, Hubble said: "No, no, it's a lot quieter than it used to be - we used to have bangers and air bombs and and screamer rockets that used to be on sale and they were withdrawn from sale."The government is considering reducing the maximum noise limit from the current 120dB, equivalent toa thunderclap, to 110dB, which is equivalent to a car horn. Hubble said a BFA assessment of firework sales shows a 50% noise reduction to 110 dB would impact up to 60% of firework sales to the general public. Lowering levels to 90DB, equivalent to a lawnmower, as some campaigners want, would affect about 95% of fireworks."That's effectively a ban on consumer fireworks, not a modest reduction in noise," he said.RSPCA advice for people with nervous pets:Stay calm and show your pet that all is wellPut on music or the TV to help mask firework soundsClose any windows and do what you can to block out both the noise and the flashesKeep your environment secure: make sure your pet can't escape if there's a sudden noiseFor dogs: let them pace around, if they're whining, barking or hiding, let themPlay with a toy if your pet wants to join in, but don't force them to playCombat Stress advice for people with PTSD:Use noise cancelling headphones to reduce the sound of explosions and blackout blinds to block out  flashes of lightUse scented candles, diffusers or plug ins to make your home smell good and nothing like those you remember from deploymentsRemind yourself you are safe, and focus on the present using breathing and grounding techniques, or with exerciseAsk friends and family to be with you on key dates like Bonfire Night

title: Would you take a test to see if your life will be cut short? I did - and it changed me
description: Image source, Katie DoyImage caption, Laura Sides faced a dilemma of whether to get tested to see if she had inherited her father's conditionByEmily D
body: Image source, Katie DoyImage caption, Laura Sides faced a dilemma of whether to get tested to see if she had inherited her father's conditionByEmily DoughtyIf you could find out if you had a gene that would cut your life short, would you?This is the dilemma Laura Sides faced when she was offered a test for the rare form of early onset dementia that her dad was diagnosed with in his 40s.Laura spoke to Dr Sian Williams, host of BBC Radio 4's Life Changing podcast, about her decision to take the test and how it has shaped the rest of her life.Growing up, Laura says she always felt close to her dad as they had a "similar nature". He was a GP and "the most amazing doting father," she says. When his Alzheimer's symptoms became more severe, Laura dropped out of university to care for him."We did have a really lovely time," she says, remembering trips to a lighthouse and collecting coasters. "I'd run him baths and just play music and pour jugs of hot water over his head and he loved it."Image source, Laura SidesImage caption, Laura had just celebrated her 21st birthday when she began caring for her dadIt was at a hospital appointment with her dad when a doctor told Laura she had a 50/50 chance of developing the same type of early onset Alzheimer's known as the "London variant". "All I could think was, that's a toss of a coin," she says. "I was still so involved with what was going on with him [her dad]. I just pushed it really, really deep down."Laura's dad died in 2009, just a year after her mum had died."All of a sudden I got such an overwhelming urge to leave," she says. So she booked a solo around-the-world trip, eventually settling in Melbourne, Australia.It was there that thoughts of inheriting her dad's condition "started creeping in" and she went to see a specialist in 2013. He told her a test could determine with 99.999% certainty if she would inherit early onset dementia. If she had the gene, her expected age of decline would be 46 to 48, he said."I just thought, I'm not there yet. I don't want to do that."Life Changing'Toss of a coin’ if I’d inherit dementia gene4 November 2026As Laura entered her 30s she found herself thinking about the test more and more and decided she wanted to know. But first, she had to undergo six months of genetic counselling."There's not many realms in life where you find out your fate and it can be very difficult information to process," she says.After a six-week wait for the test results to come through, the day finally arrived. Laura says she felt "extremely nervous". She had booked a table for lunch with a friend afterwards - but went into the appointment alone. "I said, 'Let's cut straight to it.' They said, 'We're really sorry, it's not good news, and you have inherited the gene.'" She remembers "almost a white blurry noise of just sitting there"."I came out of that room and my friend burst into hysterical tears." But Laura didn't react. "We went for our lunch and it was lovely. I don't know if it'd sunk in."The reality hit later. "I was angry. I felt it was so unjust. I was just too confused at how I was meant to live now. How do you live with that knowledge?"Image source, Laura SidesImage caption, Laura has taken part in medical trials all over the worldLaura began to feel a pull back home to the UK, especially as her sister was pregnant. "It doesn't make sense... to live on the other side of the world when she's going to have a baby."However, her around-the-world travels continued as she took part in medical trials before and after her diagnosis."It felt like such a positive to be involved in something out of such a negative situation."Image source, Laura SidesImage caption, Laura (right) is a chef and owns a cafe restaurant and catering business with two friendsLaura is now 43 - three years away from the age doctors predicted she will begin to notice symptoms."I keep waiting for something to sort of hit home. I guess one day I'll start declining but that doesn't keep me up at night."She is "grateful and so lucky for the people in her life". But meeting anyone new is hard. "Do I tell them? Do I not tell them? At what point do I tell them? "And more often than not, when I have told them, it ends." However she says she has been "proven wrong". "I have been shown I can be loved despite this. It fills my heart with reassurance and joy".  Laura says she had always "naively assumed" she would be a mother."[Its] one of the very few things that I never questioned that I'd be good at and I wanted to do. That's hard... but it doesn't make sense to do it. It wouldn't be fair."Image source, Laura SidesImage caption, Laura loves swimming and is aiming to swim in as many seas as possibleFor Laura, life is now about tapping in to things that "make her happy". "It's not about huge aspirations. It's not like I want to see the Grand Canyon... I want to have time now around the people that I adore and make me feel safe. "I love nature. I love being outside. I'm obsessed with being submerged in water. It sounds so corny, but...I believe it really is actually the little things are the big things."I hope I just have a wonderful few years in this world... drinking champagne and eating oysters - two of my favourite things."If you or someone you know has been affected by dementia, you can access support from the BBC Action Line.Get in touchHave you been affected by the issues raised in this story?Get our flagship newsletter with all the headlines you need to start the day. Sign up here.

title: Does Kane deal end Premier League career but offer England hope?
description: Harry Kane's decision to sign a new contract with Bayern Munich carries heavy significance for the Bundesliga giants, who have been celebrating his st
body: Harry Kane's decision to sign a new contract with Bayern Munich carries heavy significance for the Bundesliga giants, who have been celebrating his status as a Ballon d'Or winner, but also for England and the Premier League's record books.Bayern have acted swiftly to secure the 33-year-old on a deal taking him through to 2029 after he was crowned the world's best player, ensuring England's captain and record goalscorer will spend the final peak years of a magnificent career at Allianz Arena.Kane has written himself into Bayern legend since joining from Spurs for £86m in August 2023, scoring 102 goals in 102 Bundesliga matches, winning two league titles and three successive Golden Boot awards.It is why Bayern could not contemplate his departure as other clubs eyed his next move - and why the announcement Kane is staying casts ripples far beyond Munich.Does it mean Kane will never grace the Premier League again? And does it mean - far more enticingly - he has his sights set on two more major tournaments and two more chances to grasp the prize that has eluded him at international level?Former England striker Chris Sutton told BBC Sport: "I certainly think, although you always have to factor fitness issues into all of this, that Harry is more than capable of carrying on for a few years yet, easily."People might say his game lacks a little bit of pace, but he's so strong in other areas. He is a world-class all-round player. His finishing isn't going to be affected in any way by his age. He can still link up play and his football brain is first class."I don't see his age being such a big deal. You think of pacy players over the years who rely on that part of the game then lose it as they get older. Harry is not one of those. He seems fit and at the peak of his powers with Bayern and England."Kane's new contract expires shortly before his 36th birthday, certainly raising the prospect the player who left Spurs as the highest scorer in their history with 280 goals in 435 appearances may never grace the Premier League again.His consummate professionalism, and apparent ability to develop into the complete player with age, means this can never be discounted.The notion of an emotional return to Spurs at some point has often provided background noise, but now looks increasingly unlikely.What it surely means is that Alan Shearer will remain the Premier League's highest scorer - who knows what will happen with Erling Haaland as Manchester City await punishment after being found guilty of breaching financial regulations they deny? - and out of Kane's reach.Shearer scored 260 goals in 441 Premier League matches for Blackburn Rovers and Newcastle United. Kane scored 213 times in 320 league games for Spurs.With Kane still 47 short of Shearer's record, it would need a spectacular late-career flourish for him to eclipse the Geordie icon's tally to write another entry into the history books, which also have him as England's highest scorer with 91 goals from a record-equalling 125 caps.What will be of huge interest to Thomas Tuchel - the coach who took him to Bayern and now leads England - is that Kane has delivered a clear indication that Euro 2028, to be played in the UK and Ireland, is firmly in his sights.And, when this new deal expires, Kane is also only a year away from the 2030 World Cup, to be played in Morocco, Portugal and Spain, with special centenary opening matches held in Uruguay, Argentina, and Paraguay.This, of course, is a stretch given the inevitable rigours of age, but few who know Kane, who have watched him move to a new level at Bayern, would ever say never to such a driven personality, hiding fierce mental strength and a competitive instinct behind his humble 'anti-superstar' persona.Sutton said: "Euro 2028 certainly shouldn't be a problem and who knows beyond that? If Harry has got players around him with pace and dynamism, as well as runners in and around him, then his football brain isn't going to change and he can still play a huge part."He's such a sharp, quick, thinker. He reads the game superbly, knows where his next pass is going and has shown an ability to drop deep and impact the game."Harry just seems to be getting better and more rounded with age. And as for age, just look at someone like Teddy Sheringham. He was playing and scoring goals for West Ham United in the Premier League in his 40s."Sheringham was an incredibly talented player with supreme intelligence. Harry Kane falls right into the same category."Ronaldo has just retired from international football with Portugal at 41, but he is a totally different player than Harry Kane. Harry is one who can drop a little bit deeper to use his incredible ability and range of passing."As well as that ability, it is about how Harry's football brain works as much as anything and that won't change with age."And it is an argument, and a hope, that is even more pertinent as England still do not possess any other striker or forward who could be considered anywhere near Kane's class or potency."When you talk about 2028 or 2030, who are the English strikers coming through to challenge him to take him out of the team?" said Sutton. "There's no-one in his class or effectiveness, or anywhere near it."What also plays into the argument that Kane cannot be ruled out of such long-term involvement is the manner in which he responded so superbly to what was a disappointing Euro 2024, not only as England lost in the final to Spain but because he looked a jaded shadow of his old self.Kane looked so out of sorts there was a clamour for him to be replaced by Ollie Watkins, then at Aston Villa. He was substituted in all of England's knockout matches, including after only 61 minutes of that final loss to Spain in Berlin.And yet, Kane still finished as the tournament's joint top scorer with three goals from seven games. The notion of him being replaced with the stakes so high now is unthinkable, such is his peerless form and stature.While Bayern are convinced their new investment in Kane's brilliance will be rewarded with further honours, Tuchel will hope it is motivation and inspiration to finally end the country's long wait for international glory.

schema.headline: Does Kane deal end Premier League career but offer England hope?

title: Nvidia, SpaceX lose billions in market value as AI stocks plummet
description: Major tech firms including Nvidia, SpaceX and Tesla have lost hundreds of billions of dollars in market value, and more than $2 trillion was wiped fro
body: Major tech firms including Nvidia, SpaceX and Tesla have lost hundreds of billions of dollars in market value, and more than $2 trillion was wiped from the tech-heavy Nasdaq composite stock index in a market rout.Shares in firms across the tech and artificial intelligence sectors plummeted, partly driven by concerns of tougher regulation following Democratic wins in key data centre states.Those losses dragged the Nasdaq down by more than 5.5%, losing an estimated $2.5tn in market capitalisation, according to Dow Jones data, while other key US stock indexes also saw big losses.Following the election, some tech leaders said they needed to put more effort into marketing data centres and AI.Democrats in races across the US  campaigned to slow the onslaught of data centres and AI, and there were dozens of measures on ballots around the country aimed at restricting the development of the hubs crucial for powering the technology.Texas governor-elect Gina Hinojosa campaigned heavily against data centres, pledging a moratorium on new construction in the sector.Shares in companies heavily exposed to AI data centres, including crucial chipmakers and semiconductor manufacturers, fell sharply on Thursday, highlighting investor concerns that had already been growing.Nvidia shares slid more than 9%, knocking more than $400m off the firm's market value.Other chipmakers also suffered, with AMD and Micron both dropping by more than 17%. Intel shares also dropped, down 10.3%, while memory card maker SanDisk plunged more than 22%.The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index, which tracks the performance of 30 of the largest companies involved in semiconductor production, fell by more than 12%.Shares in Elon Musk's companies SpaceX and Tesla also plunged, falling 8% and nearly 11% respectively and shaving more than $300m off the firms' market value on Thursday.Musk had spent nearly $450m backing Republican campaigns, including at least $45m in support of Ken Paxton for the Texas senate seat, but Texas was turned blue in the Democratic tsunami on Tuesday night.The stock falls also hit other major US stock indexes. The S&P 500 index fell by 4.4% by the end of trading, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average erased gains made on Wednesday to close down more than 3.4%.The Nasdaq Composite fall was so large it is now in what market watchers call correction territory, which is where an index or company value falls at least 10% below its recent high.Susannah Streeter, chief investment strategist at Wealth Club, said the steep sell-off on the Nasdaq and the S&P 500 was sending shockwaves into other markets."Fresh panic over the AI trade has hit Wall Street hard," she said."Fears that the vast sums poured into AI infrastructure may not deliver the returns investors have been banking on are now colliding with the prospect of a sharp slowdown in data centre construction."Some tech leaders have said they were caught off guard by the backlash against data centres in the midterms.OpenAI president and co-founder Greg Brockman said he believed everyone had been surprised by the reaction to data centres, and more work needed to be done to ensure communities were on board."A lot of our shift over the course of this year has really been to realise that from San Francisco trying to build infrastructure in Texas, Georgia, and other places, you can't just tweet and say: 'This is going to be good.' You need to be in those communities," Brockman said at the WSJ Tech conference in Napa, California on Wednesday evening.Meta's president Dina Powell McCormick said that the industry needed to put more effort into selling AI as a good idea."I think we need to double and triple down on telling the story," she told the WSJ conference.Alongside the immediate impacts of the US mid-term elections, some investors have become concerned that AI shares could be in a bubble that is due a correction.

schema.headline: Nvidia, SpaceX lose billions in market value as AI stocks plummet

title: California Governor Gavin Newsom commutes sentences for state's 548 death row inmates
description: California Governor Gavin Newsom has commuted the death sentences of all 548 people on death row in the state, changing them instead to life in prison
body: California Governor Gavin Newsom has commuted the death sentences of all 548 people on death row in the state, changing them instead to life in prison. "We can now let these offenders die in obscurity while we forever remember and honour the victims," he said in a letter.The decision to spare death row inmates is largely symbolic in a state that has not executed an inmate since 2006, though experts say it could save millions of dollars in court costs each year. Only 13 inmates have been executed since voters reinstated the death penalty in 1978.The decision comes as Newsom, the Democratic leader of the most populous US state, has been discussed as a possible 2028 contender for president.Newsom, who is term limited, is winding down his final months in office. Fellow Democrat Xavier Becerra is projected to take over after the midterm elections on Tuesday. Newsom explained in his letter that he is exercising his constitutional clemency authority to commute the sentences to life without the possibility of parole. "After nearly 30 years in public office, I have come to understand the limits of what government can justly accomplish," Newsom said. "I take this action because I firmly believe that state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California's values, undermines the foundations of our legal system and diminishes each of us".California has historically had the largest population of death row inmates. Newsom had previously ordered a halt to the death penalty in the state in 2019.Newsom, describing his decision as a difficult but "righteous action", said that although many Californians feel that those who commit brutal crimes deserve to die, he has concluded that "the state cannot morally kill them".He said that by every measure, California's system for administering the death penalty "is a failure", and that it has not and cannot be fairly applied, resulting in the conviction of innocent people.Life without the possibility of parole is the most severe punishment he can lawfully impose and that the state can ethically enforce, he said.He acknowledged that his clemency action will anger and hurt some Californians and said that it will "always weigh heavily on me"."As Governor, I alone bear responsibility for this decision and its impact, just as I alone would bear responsibility for each execution," he wrote. "For this reason, I am compelled to follow my conscience and, as authorised by our Constitution, take this action for the welfare of the State of California."Because individual states have the power to prosecute crimes and order executions, much of the power lies with state governors.The decision comes after the high-profile botched execution of a woman in Tennessee in late September and while executions have been on the rise in the US. There are three executions scheduled for Thursday in Indiana, Florida and Alabama.Most of Newsom's action on Thursday will need court approval, CalMatters reported. For the commutations of the nearly 400 prisoners convicted of multiple felonies, at least four of seven judges on the California Supreme Court have to sign off.Anthony D Romero, the executive director of the American Civil Liberties Union, applauded Newsom's action."These commutations reflect what justice demands: an end to a racist, error-prone, and inhumane punishment that has burdened California for far too long," Romero said."By taking this step, Gov. Newsom has affirmed that the death penalty has no place in California and he showed real courage by confronting racialised injustice head-on."On the federal level, President Donald Trump, a long-time supporter of the death penalty, has described capital punishment as "an essential tool for deterring and punishing those who would commit the most heinous crimes and acts of lethal violence against American citizens".In 2020, during his first term, he ended a nearly two-decade moratorium on the federal death penalty, by ordering 13 executions over a six-month period.While the moratorium returned under President Biden, on the first day of Trump's second term in 2025, he signed an executive order that re-instated the death penalty. No federal executions have been carried out since he signed it, however. In the US, both the federal government and local states authorities can order executions.The death penalty is legal in 27 states, but has been abolished in 23 states and Washington DC, according to the Death Penalty Information Center, a national non-profit.California, which primarily uses lethal injection for executions, used to house male death row prisoners in San Quentin State Prison north of San Francisco, and female inmates in the Central California Women's Facility in the Central Valley. But a 2016 ballot measure allowed for their transfer to other facilities that provide a necessary level of security, according to the California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation.

schema.headline: California Governor Gavin Newsom commutes sentences for state's 548 death row inmates
